newsitem.title: USA: Coast Guard again tighten Mississippi travel rules.
newsitem.headline: Coast Guard again tighten Mississippi travel rules.

text.p: The Coast Guard Monday said travel restrictions on the Mississippi for some commercial vessels had been further tightened as conditions on the river remained hazardous

On Friday, the Coast Guard ruled that tank vessels or tank ships with 1,600 gross tons or more carrying certain petroleum products or chemicals, as well as deep-draft chemical tank ships, must travel in daylight hours only downbound between mile 233 (Baton Rouge) and mile 88 (New Orleans) of the river.

"The restrictions came into effect at noon (CST) on Saturday and we've tightened it so that ships have to be south of mile 78 by sundown," said commander Daniel Whiting of the Coast Guard Marine Safety Office.

A number of restrictions already in place, such as a sharp cut in the loads tugboat can tow and backed-up traffic at key locations such as the industrial canal lock at New Orleans, has cut commercial river traffic by around half, according to industry officials.

"We have never as an inudustry had to resort to this level of safety on the Mississippi...(and) it is significantly slowing things down," Ken Wells, southern area vice president of the Washington-based trade group American Waterways Operators, said last Friday.

The traffic restrictions are a compromise following days of discussions last week between Coast Guard officials and Louisiana governor Murphy Foster, and lobbying by large industry, especially chemical and petro-chemical concerns who are hardest hit by the restrictions.

The governor had threatened to call for much tighter restrictions, or even a temporary halt to river traffic, if conditions remained hazardous. His call came after the release of noxious fumes from a capsized barge carrying petrochemicals near government buildings in Baton Rouge.
Meanwhile, the river appeared to have stabilized for now but the fast current remained dangerous, the Coast Guard said.

"The river has flattened out and appears to have stabilized but the current is still very strong and dangerous," said Commander Whiting. "The mean current is six knots but it is much higher in specific locations."

The Mississippi is one of the world's busiest waterways, with around a half billion tons of cargo traffic a year, according to U.S. Army Corps of Engineers data. Around a quarter of that consists of oil and oil products and chemicals, the figures show.
